posts.cooked:
1. Project Overview

  • Name: Lifeboat
  • One line: a static web app that scans a CKB address (or an old MetaMask address) and, where the holder can act alone, builds the exit transaction for assets whose wallet, bridge or app is gone.
  • Problem it solves:
    • Wallets, bridges and apps on CKB shut down: Portal Wallet, Godwoken, Force Bridge, USDI, NexisDAO.
    • Their users’ assets usually stay on chain, under scripts the holder can often still satisfy. What disappears is the website that knew how to build the transaction.
    • Lifeboat shows what an address really holds. Where the holder can act alone, it builds that transaction and shows it in full before the holder signs it in their own wallet.
  • Who uses it:
    • CKB holders who used an old wallet or app and are not sure what is left: one paste of an address, nothing to install, nothing signed.
    • Reviewers and the community, through a public sheet that says, protocol by protocol, whether a holder can get out without the team.
  • Type: user safety / resilience tool, open source (MIT).
  • Repository: GitHub - ding99bt/lifeboat · GitHub
  • Live demo: https://lifeboat-ckb.vercel.app
  • What already exists: a working scanner on mainnet and testnet, a Nervos DAO exit verified end to end on a local devnet, a “Left behind” table built from the CKB Explorer, and 24 unit tests.
  • What Spark adds: the Portal Wallet move-out, reclaiming CKB from dead token cells, an exit sheet for about 10 protocols, a full testnet cycle with real wallets and 10 user sessions, and a static release on IPFS.

image2752×1348 502 KB

What is built today, and what this grant funds.

Live product screenshots

image1920×1200 318 KB

Home page. Read-only demo: nothing is signed on mainnet.

image2560×2512 347 KB

Pasting the Ethereum address once used with Portal Wallet: Lifeboat derives its pw-lock and finds 50,000 CKB under a discontinued product. Addresses are blurred in this screenshot.

image2368×1490 316 KB

A JoyID wallet with several kinds of cells, each labelled with what the holder can do. Totals match the CKB Explorer cell by cell.

image2560×1972 318 KB

CKB still under the scripts of products that are gone or changed, reproducible with npm run snapshot.

2. Team Profile

  • Applicant: Ding, GitHub: ding99bt
  • Role: author and maintainer of Lifeboat.
  • Background: software engineer, 3+ years at Samsung R&D; researched the Stellar blockchain before moving to CKB.
  • Why me: Lifeboat is not an idea on paper. The scanner and the Nervos DAO exit already run, and every number in this proposal can be reproduced from the repository. I want to take it to the point where a holder of a dead product’s cells can get out on their own.
  • How I work: nothing is taken on trust.
    • Every scan is checked against the CKB Explorer (npm run compare).
    • Every transaction recipe runs end to end on a local devnet before testnet, with checks that fail when something is wrong.
    • Nothing signs on mainnet before review.
  • Project repository: GitHub - ding99bt/lifeboat · GitHub
  • Contact: Telegram @ding0x68

3. Project Background

When a CKB product shuts down, its users’ @ding0x68ells stay on chain. Some can be moved by the holder alone; some need the operator; for many, nobody has checked. Every time so far, the fix was a one-off, or nothing:

  • NexisDAO’s frontend shut down abruptly, and a community developer had to build dCKB Rescuer, an alternative frontend just for dCKB withdrawals (t/8369).
  • Godwoken and Force Bridge were sunset. After the exit window, Godwoken leftovers can no longer be withdrawn through its usual front end (t/8789).
  • USDI on CKB was discontinued (t/10417).
  • Portal Wallet’s site, ckb.pw, now redirects to an unrelated domain; its maintainers already had no capacity in 2023 (t/7008).

Live cells per script, from the CKB Explorer API (npm run snapshot, 17 Nov 2026):

image2272×632 76.2 KB

Spark’s Q3 report noted that few projects deal with what happens when centralized services stop responding or entry points are closed, and asked for practical work on it (t/11077). Lifeboat addresses exactly that disruption: the operator disappears (frontend, domain, wallet app or server) while the assets remain on chain.

Scenario. Someone deposited CKB into the Nervos DAO with Portal Wallet in 2021. Today they paste their old MetaMask address into Lifeboat. It shows the pw-lock cells and the deposit, explains that the deposit must be withdrawn first, builds each transaction, and MetaMask signs it. No team, server or custodian is needed.

4. Solution

Lifeboat runs entirely in the browser and talks to a CKB node directly (public nodes or the user’s own). It never holds keys or funds.

image2752×1344 395 KB

  • Scan: a CKB address, an old MetaMask address (its pw-lock and Omnilock addresses are derived, nothing is connected), or a wallet connected through CCC (JoyID, MetaMask, UniSat, OKX, UTXO Global…).
  • Label: every lock and type script gets a name and a status from CCC’s known scripts, the CKB Explorer’s script list and Lifeboat’s own dated notes (active / discontinued / not checked).
  • Report: CKB per group, what sits under a discontinued product, and what the holder can do.
  • Get out: an exit recipe builds the transaction and shows it in full: what it spends, what it creates, whether each output belongs to the user, and the fee. The user signs in their own wallet.

How it differs from what exists:

  • Neuron can close an empty sUDT account to recover its CKB, and offers a manual troubleshooting page for non-empty ones (t/7827): Neuron users only, sUDT only. Lifeboat is wallet-agnostic and covers xUDT.
  • The CCC demo app can sign almost anything, but it does not explain what each cell is or warn that a product is gone.
  • dCKB Rescuer solved one protocol once: 10 depositors took back 24 deposits (1.43M CKB) through it, and it stopped working in 2025 (https://talk.nervos.org/t/11016). Lifeboat is a registry of exits, plus a sheet that rates every protocol on whether a holder can leave alone.
  • secnev ( Spark Program | secnev — CKB-native risk observatory ) scores market and stablecoin risk. Tranfr ( Tranfr — Programmable Recovery for CKB ) and InheritVault ( InheritVault - A Simple Timelock Inheritance Vault on Nervos CKB (Web MVP) ) are recovery plans set up before anything goes wrong; Waymark ( Waymark — Recovering useful wallet state without starting from zero ) restores a wallet’s sync state. Lifeboat handles assets already stranded by a lost operator. These complement each other.

Explicitly out of scope: exits that need the operator (Godwoken leftovers, Force Bridge leftovers, USDI redemption); mainnet signing before review; an audit; an in-browser light client (stretch goal only).

5. Technical Approach

  • Stack: Vite, React, TypeScript, CCC (core library 1.23.1 and the CCC connector), Tailwind. Static build with relative paths, so it can be served from IPFS. Vitest for unit tests; a Node script for end-to-end runs.
  • Reading cells: findCellsByLock per lock, with data. A lock with more cells than the reading limit is cut short, but its Nervos DAO cells are always read in full. This was a real bug found on the way, now covered by a regression test.
  • Labels: CCC known scripts per network, the CKB Explorer list (keyed by type hash when there is one, because the same binary can be deployed twice: USDI is a deployment of the xUDT binary), and curated notes with dates and links.
  • Checks against the chain: npm run compare – scans with Lifeboat’s own code and compares every lock’s balance and cell count with the CKB Explorer. It matched on four real mainnet wallets, the largest with 183 cells.

Nervos DAO exit (built, verified on a devnet)

image2752×1166 382 KB

The recipe follows RFC 0023 and CCC’s own Nervos DAO module. On testnet and mainnet, the claim opens about 30 days after a deposit, so Lifeboat ships a local devnet with 10-block epochs where the full cycle takes about 6 minutes. npm run e2e:dao runs it with checks:

  • an early claim is refused by the node;
  • the claim’s fee is a few hundred shannons, so the compensation is not paid as fee;
  • the outputs receive every input shannon minus the fee.

The same builders are used by the UI.

image2368×762 89 KB

Each deposit shows its compensation and when it could be claimed. The action appears only for the connected owner, and only on testnet or the devnet.

image1440×1302 99.4 KB

Before signing: every cell spent and created, “yours” or “NOT your address” on each output, and the fee.

image2368×762 84.3 KB

After phase 1: the claim button counts down to the end of the 180-epoch cycle.

image1440×1044 71.3 KB

Phase 2: the deposit plus its compensation go back to the owner as plain CKB.

image1440×1170 68.8 KB

Committed on chain (devnet).

Portal Wallet move-out (funded by this grant)

image2752×936 346 KB

pw-lock checks an Ethereum signature. CCC’s EVM signer already derives the pw-lock address of a MetaMask account and signs pw-lock witnesses. Lifeboat will use it to move pw-lock cells to a lock the holder uses today (the Omnilock of the same MetaMask account, or another address they choose), with the same full preview. Nervos DAO deposits under pw-lock are withdrawn first. Testnet first (pw-lock is deployed on testnet, and CCC knows its deployment); mainnet only after review.

Hardest part. Making sure a holder cannot be tricked into signing something else. Every output is checked against the locks the connected wallet controls and flagged in the preview. The build is static and published with its IPFS CID, with no backend, so there is nothing to compromise between the user and the chain.

6. To-Do List (6 weeks, about 10 hours a week)

  • Week 1:
    • Make a Nervos DAO deposit and phase 1 on testnet with JoyID and with MetaMask, which starts the ~30-day clock.
    • Publish the static build on IPFS (CID), next to the live demo.
    • Agree the exit-sheet list with the committee.
    • Start recruiting testers.
  • Week 2:
    • Portal Wallet move-out on testnet: fund a pw-lock cell from a MetaMask account, build the move-out with CCC’s EVM signer, preview, sign.
    • Tokens under pw-lock.
    • Unit tests.
  • Week 3:
    • Reclaim CKB from dead token cells (sUDT/xUDT): typed confirmation, a plain warning that burning gives up any claim, and “not reclaimable” when a token’s rules forbid it.
    • Tests.
  • Week 4:
    • Exit sheet, about 10 entries (page + JSON). Each answers four questions, with links to code or a transaction:
    • Can a holder exit without the team?
    • Can the code be replaced?
    • Does an operator key gate exits?
    • Which server or frontend does the exit depend on?
    • Research note on FlashSigner and UniPass v3: can holders still sign?
  • Week 5:
    • 10 user sessions (Nervos Nation, CKBFans, builder groups), including former Portal Wallet users if we can find them.
    • Fix what they find.
  • Week 6:
    • Claim the week-1 testnet deposits (phase 2) with the same wallets.
    • Final report, a short demo video, release v0.2 on IPFS.

7. Required Funding and Breakdown

image1780×542 40.9 KB

8. Deliverables and How to Verify (no code review required)

Deliverables:

  • Public repository (MIT) with the scanner, the three recipes (Nervos DAO, Portal Wallet move-out, dead-token reclaim), the label registry and tests.
  • A static release on IPFS with its CID, next to the live demo at https://lifeboat-ckb.vercel.app.
  • The exit sheet: page + JSON, about 10 entries with sources.
  • Testnet transaction hashes: DAO deposit, phase 1 (week 1) and phase 2 (week 6) with real wallets; a pw-lock move-out signed with MetaMask.
  • A short report on FlashSigner and UniPass v3.
  • Notes from the 10 user sessions, including what failed.

How to verify:

  • Open the live demo (https://lifeboat-ckb.vercel.app) and paste any address. Its totals must match the CKB Explorer. Or run npm run compare – , which prints MATCH or MISMATCH per lock.
  • Run the Nervos DAO cycle on a devnet: npm run devnet:up && npm run e2e:dao. It prints every transaction hash and its checks.
  • Open the testnet transaction hashes in the final report on the testnet explorer: deposit, phase 1, phase 2, move-out.
  • Reproduce the “Left behind” numbers with npm run snapshot.
  • Rebuild the static app with npm ci && npm run build and compare the IPFS CID.
  • Read the exit sheet: every answer links to code or a transaction. Disagreements go to a GitHub issue.

9. Current State vs. Funded Work

image2432×726 82 KB

10. CKB Alignment

  • It answers Spark’s own Q3 question about centralized services that stop responding, with a specific disruption (the operator disappears) and measurable stakes (the table in section 3).
  • It is possible because of the Cell model: every cell names the lock and type that rule it, so “what do I own, and how do I get it out” can be answered generically, and state rent means every abandoned cell still holds CKB the holder can reclaim.
  • It builds on CCC (wallet connectors, known scripts, the EVM signer, Nervos DAO helpers) instead of re-implementing signing.
  • After Spark: a Community Fund DAO proposal for mainnet signing after review, wider protocol coverage, and maintenance of the exit sheet with protocol teams.

Questions we expect

Is it safe to sign with Lifeboat? It never holds keys. Every transaction is shown in full and checked against the connected wallet’s own locks before signing. In this grant, signing is on testnet only, and mainnet signing waits for review.

Why not just use Neuron or the CCC demo? They can sign, but they do not tell a holder that a product is gone, what each cell is, or what the safe sequence is (for example, withdraw a DAO deposit under pw-lock before moving it). Lifeboat is that guidance, plus the transactions.

What about funds only the operator can release? Lifeboat shows them, says so plainly, and links the official process. It never offers to “recover” them.

Why a devnet? On testnet, a Nervos DAO claim opens about 30 days after a deposit. The devnet makes the full cycle checkable in minutes; the testnet cycle is still run during the grant, from week 1 to week 6.

posts.cooked:
One question I expect, so I’ll answer it up front: apps built on CCC can already sign for pw-lock cells, so what does Lifeboat add?

They can, and Lifeboat uses the same CCC signer. Signing is not the missing piece. Knowing is. When a MetaMask account is connected, CCC includes its pw-lock address, so an app like app.ckbccc.com can spend those cells, and NervDAO handles Nervos DAO deposits for a connected wallet. But a holder only gets there if they already know that their old CKB is still on chain, that it sits under pw-lock (the lock behind Portal Wallet, whose site is gone), and that a Nervos DAO deposit under it has to be withdrawn before the CKB can move. Today nothing tells them that.

I checked how much this is about, using the public mainnet RPC (get_cells on the pw-lock code hash)

  • 29,219 live pw-lock cells hold 281.8M CKB across 8,011 addresses.
  • 6,700 of these addresses (84%), holding 141.6M CKB, have no live cell newer than 1 Jan 2024. 1,802 of them hold at least 1,000 CKB.
  • 2,611 of the cells are Nervos DAO cells (172.5M CKB), which need the two-step withdrawal before they can move.

Idle does not mean lost. Some of these holders keep long-term DAO deposits and know exactly where their CKB is. For the others, the first step is to find out what is there, and that is what the live demo already does, read-only and without connecting anything: paste an Ethereum address at https://lifeboat-ckb.vercel.app and it derives the pw-lock address, lists what is there and names the product it belonged to.

So I see it like this: NervDAO is for managing your DAO deposits from a wallet you know is yours, and the CCC app is a toolbox for developers and experienced users. Lifeboat is for a holder who is not sure what is left. It finds the assets, explains them and walks through a safe exit with a full preview. For a product that is gone, there is no original team left to build that exit, and Lifeboat reuses CCC for signing instead of competing with it.

posts.cooked:
A second question I expect, about safety: should a third-party tool be building exit transactions for other people’s assets at all?

For a product that is gone, there is nobody else left to do it. The original team has stopped, so the real choice is between a public, reviewable tool and each holder piecing together raw transactions alone. Lifeboat is built to keep that risk small:

  • It never holds keys or funds. The holder signs in their own wallet.
  • Every transaction is shown in full before signing, and each output is checked against the locks the connected wallet controls, so anything going to an address that is not theirs is flagged.
  • In this grant, signing happens on testnet only. Mainnet signing waits for review.
  • Exits that need the operator (Godwoken or Force Bridge leftovers, USDI redemption) are labelled as such. Lifeboat points to the official process and never offers to “recover” them.
  • The code is open (MIT), and the release will be a static build published with its IPFS CID, so anyone can check that what they run matches the repository.

If the committee would prefer a narrower first step, for example read-only scanning plus the exit sheet, with transaction building kept on testnet until a review, I’m happy to adjust the scope.
